title: Transpiration & its factors
examples: What happens to transpiration when the air is very dry?
How do stomata control water loss in plants?

explain.say: Today we learn about transpiration in plants.
Stomata are tiny pores mostly on the underside of leaves. They help plants breathe and release water vapor.

draw.text: Stomata: Leaf pores for gas exchange

explain.say: A potometer measures the rate of water loss from a plant shoot. It helps us measure transpiration accurately.
Light intensity affects transpiration because it causes stomata to open wider. More light means more gas exchange.
Wind speed increases transpiration because it blows away the humid boundary layer near the leaf. This maintains a steep water vapor gradient.

items: Still Air → High Humidity → Slow Transpiration
Wind Blows → Low Humidity → Fast Transpiration

draw.text: Wind: Removes humid air, increases rate

explain.say: Humidity is the amount of water in the air. Low humidity causes transpiration to increase because the air can hold more water vapor.

draw.text: Humidity: Low air moisture, high rate

faq.q: Why is transpiration sometimes called 'plant sweating'?
faq.a: It is called sweating because the process involves the release of water vapor through pores, similar to how sweat evaporates from skin.
asks: What is the process of water loss through leaves?

faq.q: Does transpiration always cause water loss for the plant?
faq.a: While it is water loss, it is essential for creating the pull that moves water and minerals up from the roots.
asks: Is losing water bad for plants?
What is the purpose of transpiration?

faq.q: If the air is very dry, will the plant lose too much water?
faq.a: Yes, very low humidity increases the water potential gradient, causing the plant to lose water rapidly, which can cause wilting.
asks: How does humidity affect water loss?

faq.q: What is the role of the guard cells in stomata?
faq.a: The guard cells control the size of the stomatal pore by changing their own internal pressure. This allows the plant to open or close the pores.
asks: How do stomata open and close?

faq.q: Can the potometer measure transpiration directly?
faq.a: No, it measures the rate of water uptake, which is used as an indirect measure of transpiration.
asks: Does the potometer measure water loss?
What does the potometer actually measure?

facts: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plant leaves and stems.
Stomata are pores, usually on the underside of the leaf, that control gas exchange.
Increased wind speed generally increases the rate of transpiration.
Low air humidity increases the rate of transpiration because the air is drier.

quiz.say: If a plant is placed in a very dry, windy environment, what is the expected effect on its transpiration rate?
quiz.why: Low humidity and high wind speed both create a strong gradient, pulling water out of the leaf faster.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because both dry air and wind increase the rate of water loss.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because environmental factors like wind change the rate significantly.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because the combined effect of both factors is a significant increase.

quiz.say: Which structure controls the opening and closing of the stomata?
quiz.why: The guard cells surrounding the pore actively control the opening and closing of the stomata.

wrong.0: These bundles transport water, they do not control the pores.
wrong.2: These cells are inside the leaf and are involved in photosynthesis, not pore control.
wrong.3: The epidermis is the outer layer, but the guard cells are the specific regulators.

quiz.say: If the air around a plant is saturated with water vapour, what will happen to transpiration?
quiz.why: Saturated air means the air cannot hold much more water, so the water potential gradient is weak, slowing transpiration.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because humidity is a major factor affecting the rate.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because the air is already holding the maximum amount of water vapor.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because high humidity reduces the gradient between leaf and air.
